title: Interference, Diffraction & Polarization — 60 MCQs
description: 60 questions covering interference (Young's double-slit), diffraction (single slit, grating, resolving power) and polarization (phenomenon, transverse nature, Brewster's law). Options are shuffled each load and the correct choice is tracked accordingly.

questions.q: Interference is the phenomenon when two or more waves:
options: Superpose to produce a resultant amplitude distribution
questions.explanation: Interference arises when waves superpose; depending on phase relation they add constructively or destructively.

questions.q: Coherent sources are essential for stable interference because they:
questions.explanation: Coherence requires stable phase relationship (and typically same frequency), so interference pattern is stable in time.

questions.q: In Young's double-slit experiment the fringe separation (bright to bright) on screen is given by:
questions.explanation: Fringe spacing β = λ D / d where λ is wavelength, D distance to screen, d slit separation.

questions.q: For Young's double slit, the path difference for nth order bright fringe is:
questions.explanation: Constructive interference occurs when path difference = n λ (n integer) producing bright fringes.

questions.q: If slit separation d is doubled in Young's experiment (other parameters fixed), fringe width β:
questions.explanation: β = λ D / d; doubling d halves β.

questions.q: In Young's experiment, if wavelength increases, fringes:
questions.explanation: β ∝ λ so larger wavelength gives larger fringe separation.

questions.q: If the screen distance D is increased, keeping λ and d constant, fringe width:
questions.explanation: β = λD/d, so β increases linearly with D.

questions.q: If the two slits have unequal intensities, the interference pattern:
options: Has reduced contrast (visibility) but fringes remain at same positions
questions.explanation: Unequal amplitudes reduce visibility (contrast) but positions determined by phase still follow same relation.

questions.q: The condition for destructive interference (dark fringe) in Young's double slit is path difference:
questions.explanation: Destructive interference when path difference = (n + 1/2)λ.

questions.q: Fringe visibility (contrast) is defined using I_max and I_min as:
questions.explanation: Visibility V = (I_max - I_min)/(I_max + I_min) measures fringe contrast.

questions.q: Two sources are said to be temporally coherent when:
options: They maintain a fixed phase relation over time
They are at same spatial location
questions.explanation: Temporal coherence requires constant phase relation over time between waves of same frequency.

questions.q: Spatial coherence refers to:
options: Phase correlation between points across a wavefront
questions.explanation: Spatial coherence concerns correlation between phases at different spatial points on a wavefront; necessary for producing interference over finite separation.

questions.q: Young's experiment performed with white light shows fringes that:
options: Show central white fringe with colored fringes on either side
Disappear because white light is incoherent
questions.explanation: White light contains many wavelengths; central fringe (zero path difference) is white, other fringes show spectral dispersion (colored) producing overlapping colored bands.

questions.q: In thin-film interference constructive interference for reflected light occurs when the optical path difference equals:
questions.explanation: Constructive interference when effective path difference (including any π phase shifts upon reflection) equals mλ.

questions.q: Michelson interferometer measures small lengths by converting change in length to:
questions.explanation: Displacement of mirror changes optical path difference, producing fringe shifts; counting fringes yields length change (ΔL = m λ / 2).

questions.q: Diffraction is the phenomenon in which waves:
options: Bend around obstacles and spread through apertures
Always travel in straight lines without spreading
Increase in frequency on passing obstacle
questions.explanation: Diffraction is wave bending and spreading that occurs when a wave encounters obstacles or openings comparable to its wavelength.

questions.q: Single-slit diffraction pattern central maximum is:
options: Wider and more intense than secondary maxima
questions.explanation: The central maximum is the brightest and usually about twice as wide as the side maxima (for single-slit Fraunhofer diffraction).

questions.q: For a single slit of width a, minima occur at angles θ given by:
questions.explanation: Single-slit minima: a sin θ = n λ for integer n (nonzero integer), with central maximum between first minima.

questions.q: The angular width of central maximum in single slit is approximately:
questions.explanation: For small angles first minima at ± λ / a, so central maximum angular width ≈ 2 λ/a.

questions.q: Fraunhofer diffraction applies when:
options: Source and screen are effectively at infinite distance (parallel rays) or lenses are used
Source is very near to slit (Fresnel zone)
questions.explanation: Fraunhofer (far-field) diffraction assumes plane wave incidence and screen in far field or appropriate lens configuration.

questions.q: Rayleigh criterion for resolving two point sources by a circular aperture uses:
questions.explanation: Rayleigh criterion: minimum resolvable angle ≈ 1.22 λ / D for circular aperture (first zero of Airy disk).

questions.q: Diffraction grating maxima occur when d sin θ = n λ, where d is grating spacing. The integer n corresponds to:
questions.explanation: The constructive interference condition for a grating gives maxima at orders n satisfying d sin θ = n λ.

questions.q: If grating has N slits illuminated, intensity of principal maxima scales approximately as:
questions.explanation: Interference from N equally spaced coherent slits gives principal maxima intensity ∝ N² (sharpness increases with N).

questions.q: For diffraction grating, increasing number of lines per mm results in:
options: Greater angular dispersion (larger separation between spectral lines)
questions.explanation: Higher line density (smaller d) increases angular separation for given order and wavelength (sinθ = nλ/d).

questions.q: Resolving power R of a grating is given by R = λ/Δλ ≈ nN where n is order and N is total number of illuminated slits. This means resolving power increases with:
options: Order and number of slits illuminated
questions.explanation: R ≈ nN shows higher order or more illuminated slits gives better ability to distinguish close wavelengths.

questions.q: In single-slit diffraction, position y_n of nth minima on screen at distance D is approximately:
questions.explanation: Using small-angle approximation sinθ ≈ y/D, minima condition a sinθ = n λ => y_n = n λ D / a.

questions.q: If slit width a decreases, the diffraction pattern central maximum:
questions.explanation: Smaller slit width increases diffraction (wider central maximum) because λ/a larger.

questions.q: Diffraction explains why we can hear someone around a corner because sound wavelengths are:
options: Comparable to obstacle sizes causing significant diffraction
questions.explanation: When wavelength is comparable to object aperture/obstacle sizes, waves diffract and spread into shadowed regions — sound (longer λ) diffracts more than light.

questions.q: The central maximum intensity in single-slit diffraction is proportional to:
options: a² (slit width squared) for given illumination per unit width
questions.explanation: Total transmitted power ∝ a; central peak amplitude ∝ a, so intensity (∝ amplitude²) scales roughly as a² (for comparable illumination per unit width).

A transmission grating of 5000 lines per meter (d = 2×10⁻4 m) in first order gives angle for λ=500 nm as sinθ = λ/d. θ ≈
Grating is preferred over prism for spectral analysis because:
options: Grating dispersion is linear in wavelength and can give higher resolving power for many slits
questions.explanation: Gratings offer predictable angular dispersion and high resolving power proportional to number of illuminated grooves.

questions.q: Diffraction limit of an optical instrument determines:
options: Smallest angular separation it can resolve (Rayleigh criterion)
questions.explanation: Diffraction limit (set by aperture) sets resolving power; below that two point sources are not distinctly resolvable.

questions.q: Which gives best resolution (smallest resolvable angle) for an instrument with aperture diameter D?
options: Large D and short λ (θ_min ≈ 1.22 λ/D)
questions.explanation: θ_min scales as λ/D, so large aperture and small wavelength give best angular resolution.

questions.q: When white light is used with a grating, spectral orders may overlap. To avoid overlap one can:
options: Use lower orders or wavelength filters
questions.explanation: Order overlap can be avoided by restricting spectral range (filters) or using appropriate order selection; grating equation gives overlapping orders for different wavelengths.

questions.q: Polarization of light describes the:
options: Orientation of electric field vector oscillations
questions.explanation: Polarization refers to the direction (and phase relations) of the transverse E-field oscillation for electromagnetic waves.

questions.q: Unpolarized light consists of:
questions.explanation: Unpolarized light has many random polarization orientations on timescales relevant to detection.

questions.q: Polarizers transmit light whose electric field is aligned with their transmission axis and absorb/reflect perpendicular components. A pair of ideal polarizers at 90° gives transmitted intensity:
questions.explanation: Two crossed ideal polarizers block all light as second polarizer's axis is perpendicular to transmitted component.

questions.q: Malus's law states transmitted intensity I through a polarizer for incident polarized light I0 is:
questions.explanation: Malus's law: transmitted intensity = I0 cos²θ where θ is angle between incident polarization and polarizer axis.

questions.q: Brewster's angle θ_B for no reflected p-polarized light satisfies:
options: tan θ_B = n2/n1 (incident from medium n1 to n2)
questions.explanation: Brewster's law: tan θ_B = n2 / n1 (when light travels from medium 1 into medium 2) causing reflected light to be fully s-polarized.

questions.q: At Brewster's angle the reflected and refracted rays are:
options: At right angles (90°) to each other
questions.explanation: At Brewster's angle reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular; this geometric condition yields tan θ_B = n2/n1.

questions.q: Polaroid filters are commonly based on:
questions.explanation: Polaroids use aligned dichroic molecules that preferentially absorb one polarization direction, transmitting the orthogonal component.

questions.q: Circular polarization can be formed by:
options: Passing linearly polarized light through a quarter-wave plate at 45° to axis
questions.explanation: Quarter-wave plate introduces 90° phase shift between orthogonal components, generating circular polarization when amplitudes equal and axes at 45°.

questions.q: Polarization by reflection is strongest for light polarized:
options: Perpendicular to the plane of incidence (s-polarized)
questions.explanation: At Brewster's angle the p-component is not reflected, so reflected light is predominantly s-polarized (perpendicular to plane of incidence).

questions.q: Polarization confirms transverse nature of light because:
options: Only transverse waves can have a direction of oscillation (polarization) perpendicular to propagation
Polarization is unrelated to wave nature
questions.explanation: Polarization demonstrates the vector (transverse) nature of light's electric field; longitudinal waves cannot exhibit polarization transverse to propagation.

questions.q: A quarter-wave plate introduces a phase shift of:
questions.explanation: Quarter-wave plate gives a π/2 phase delay, converting linear to circular or elliptical polarization depending on input orientation.

questions.q: If unpolarized light of intensity I0 passes through an ideal polarizer, transmitted intensity is:
questions.explanation: An ideal polarizer transmits half the power of unpolarized light on average (I = I0/2).

questions.q: When two linear polarizers are crossed (90°), inserting a third polarizer at 45° between them results in transmitted intensity:
questions.explanation: Middle polarizer projects polarization and allows some light through second polarizer (quantified by successive cos² factors), demonstrating interference of polarization states.

questions.q: Brewster's angle for light from air (n≈1.00) into glass (n≈1.5) is approximately:
Which technique can determine polarization state of light?
options: Using analyzer (polarizer) and rotating it to measure intensity variation
questions.explanation: Rotating an analyzer and recording transmitted intensity reveals polarization via Malus's law; variation indicates polarization angle and type.

questions.q: Polarization by scattering (e.g., sky polarization) occurs because:
options: Scattered light has preferential polarization perpendicular to scattering plane
questions.explanation: Rayleigh scattering polarizes sunlight; scattered light tends to be polarized perpendicular to the plane containing incident and scattered rays.

questions.q: A beam of circularly polarized light passing through a linear polarizer yields an intensity independent of polarizer angle and equal to:
questions.explanation: Circularly polarized light has equal amplitude components in all linear polarization directions; transmitted intensity through linear polarizer = I/2.

questions.q: If reflected light from a dielectric surface at Brewster's angle is observed, its polarization is:
questions.explanation: At Brewster's angle p-polarized component is not reflected; reflected light is predominantly s-polarized.

questions.q: Which material is commonly used to make high-quality quarter-wave plates in visible range?
questions.explanation: Birefringent crystals like quartz or mica produce reliable retardation plates (quarter-wave) due to anisotropic refractive indices.

questions.q: A polarizer and analyzer crossed transmit no light. Introducing a half-wave plate between them rotates polarization by 90°. Resulting transmission is:
questions.explanation: Half-wave plate rotates linear polarization direction by twice the angle between input axis and fast axis; with proper rotation it can align polarization to analyzer allowing transmission.

options: Reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular
questions.explanation: The zero of p-polarized reflection coefficient occurs when reflected and refracted rays are at 90°, leading to Brewster's condition.
